                               PUC DOCKET NUMBER 59475

                          SOAH DOCKET NUMBER 473-26-16349

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                          §
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC                       §              BEFORE THE STATE
AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICE                       §
CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR                          §                     OFFICE OF
CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND                     §
NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY                       §               ADMINISTRATIVE
EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL                             §
SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION                      §                      HEARINGS
LINE PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,                       §
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,                          §
LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH,                            §
MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA,                     §
SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND                          §
WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                                 §



     FIRST AMENDED LEIF ALLRED AND LAURA PRESSLEY’S JOINT BRIEF ON
         PUBLIC UTILTY COMMISSION OF TEXAS REMAND REGARDING
                      PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE 13

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

         COMES NOW, Leif Allred and Laura Pressley, Ph.D. pro se intervenors, filing this Joint

Brief to address two preliminary order issues, namely Preliminary Order Issue 13, filed by the

Public Utility Commission in the above referenced docket and shows as follows that Applicants

offered no evidence of congestion-cost savings leaving PURA’s Consumer-protection mandate

unmet:

                    I. THE LEGISLATURE PUT CONSUMERS FIRST,
                       AND PURA § 37.056(C)(1) SAYS SO PLAINLY

1.       The Legislature did not bury its consumer-protection command in some statutory attic.

PURA says it outright: the Commission must consider “the effect of the granting of the certificate

on the cost to consumers.” Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(1).
 2.     That requirement is not advisory. It is compulsory. And Issue 13—“What are the estimated

congestion-cost savings for consumers?”—is the Commission’s way of ensuring that utilities do

not ask Texans to bankroll billion-dollar transmission projects on faith alone. The law demands

numbers, not notions.

             II. Applicants Offered No Numbers—No Congestion-Cost Savings,
                          No Rate Impacts, No Economic Modeling

3.     Applicants’ evidentiary showing on Issue 13 is not thin; it is nonexistent. They did not

quantify congestion-cost savings. They did not model rate impacts. They did not calculate resistive

losses over a 200-plus-mile 765-kV line. They did not present any economic analysis and impact

to consumers for Import Path 2 at all.

4.     The SOAH ALJs put it bluntly: Applicants “did not present any quantified congestion-cost

savings.”1 A transmission project of this magnitude demands rigorous consumer-impact analysis.

Instead, Applicants offered a void.

                    III. ERCOT’s Recommendation Cannot Fill the Void
                      Because ERCOT Did Not Study Congestion Costs

5.     Applicants lean heavily on ERCOT’s Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP), but ERCOT

itself testified that the PBRP was not an economic study. It did not evaluate congestion-cost

savings. It did not model consumer rate impacts. It did not verify the load forecast it relied upon.

And ERCOT later sought to revise that forecast downward.




1 PFD, ISSUE 13; 59475_6441_1676003.PDF.
 6.         A recommendation unsupported by substantiated load and quantified consumer benefits is

not entitled to “great weight.” It is entitled to exactly the weight the record gives it: none on Issue

13.

7.         As Justice Willett has written, courts “do not exalt form over substance”2 and the ALJs and

the Commission should not either. This is a reminder that legal actors must satisfy the actual

requirements of the law, not merely gesture toward them with superficial compliance. It is a

principle rooted in fidelity to statutory purpose, constitutional structure, and evidentiary rigor. A

reliability study cannot be repurposed into an economic justification simply because Applicants

wish it so. Legal obligations must be met in reality, not appearance. A party cannot satisfy a

statutory requirement by offering something that looks like compliance but lacks the actual content

the law demands. The ALJs and the Commission must evaluate what the evidence is, not what the

party labels it. A document titled “economic analysis” that contains no economics is not an

economic analysis.

                         IV. Intervenors Allred and Pressley Supplied Evidence
                               Showing Why the Missing Analysis Matters

8.         Intervenors—including Allred and Pressley—introduced evidence demonstrating that

Applicants’ omission is not a clerical oversight but a substantive failure:

                        a) Applicants provided no engineering data—no impedance, no MW flow,
                           no transfer-capability modeling—that would allow congestion-cost
                           analysis.3
                        b) PUC Staff witness Poole did not and could not supply basic electrical
                           parameters necessary for any economic model. 4,5




2 Zaatari v. City of Austin, 2019 WL 6336187, at 15 (Tex. 2019) (Willett, J., concurring)
3 Allred   and Pressley Initial Brief paragraphs 14-19.
4 Transcript of Hearing on Merits, June 9, 2026, p. 276, line 20 through p. 278 line 2 ; Transcript of Hearing on

Merits, June 9, 2026, p. 278 lines 4-12; Transcript of Hearing on Merits, June 9, 2026, p. 278 lines 13 -17.
5 These issues were previously raised in Allred and Pressley Initial Brief paragraphs 14-19.
                         c) Applicants did not rebut evidence of 39+ GW of planned or announced
                           generation in the Permian Basin and surrounding regions—generation that
                           could materially reduce congestion without a 765-kV line.6
                        d) Applicants did not analyze alternatives, even though alternatives directly
                           affect congestion-cost savings.

9.         Specifically, pro se intervenors, Allred and Pressley raised the issue in their Initial Brief

that congestion cost savings is never mentioned in LCRA and Oncor Joint Application. 7 As

reiterated here, Oncor and LCRA’s Joint Application provides the cost of the project, but is silent

on the estimated costs consumers will see in their monthly electric bills and these facts are

important for this proposed project and consumers over a period of time. It appears Applicants

want a blank check from consumers.

10.        Federal and state laws (such as the Federal Power Act) require electricity rates to be just

and reasonable. A project cannot be deemed genuinely "needed" if its multi-billion dollar price tag

- such as the massive 765-kV build-outs proposed in regions like Texas—results in unjustifiable

and unprecedented rate spikes for residential and commercial consumers.

11.        ALJs must weigh long-term financial benefits against initial capital expenditures. They

use these cost models to verify if the 765-kV lines will effectively reduce energy congestion or

line losses enough to produce actual long-term savings for consumers.

12.        Because amortized utility transmission costs are passed directly onto consumers' utility

bills, understanding these specific costs—often exceeding hundreds of dollars per year for average

households—ensures that vulnerable consumers are not disproportionately burdened by grid-

expansion projects.




6 PFD findings; 59475_6441_1676003.PDF
7 Allred   and Pressley Initial Br. at paragraphs 21-23, 30-32 (June 19,2026).
 13.     The PUC initially required Question 13 to be answered for this project:

        Cost to Consumers - 13. What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that
        may result from the proposed transmission facilities considering both current and future
        expected congestion levels and the ability of the proposed transmission facilities to reduce
        those congestion levels?

14.     In reviewing Oncor and LCRA’s 2,870 pages of their Joint Application, the words

“congestion cost savings” do not exist. The Application is lacking consumer cost transparency for

this project as required by PUC’s Order of Referral and Preliminary Order Question 13, and said

information was not subsequently provided through witness testimony.

15.     The ALJs justly concluded that Applicants “did not meet their burden.”8 That is judicial

understatement. They did not shoulder the burden at all related to Issue 13.

  V. Without Congestion-Cost Evidence, the Commission Cannot Lawfully Find “Need”

16.     PURA’s consumer-cost requirement is not optional. It is a statutory prerequisite to granting

a CCN. When a utility seeks to impose billions in new transmission costs on Texans, the

Commission must know—must be shown—what consumers gain in return.

17.     Here, the record contains:

                   a) zero quantified congestion-cost savings,
                   b) zero rate-impact analysis,
                   c) zero economic modeling, and
                   d) zero evidence of consumer cost benefit.

18.     To call this evidentiary record “insufficient” would be charitable. It is empty. And an empty

record cannot support a finding of “need.”




8 PDF page 35
 19.      As Justice Willett has observed, “Text is the law, and the law must be followed.” 9 The

Legislature’s words—not agency preferences, not policy aspirations, not convenience—govern.

Agencies cannot stretch statutes beyond their textual limits and courts must enforce the law as

written, not as wished. Parties cannot satisfy statutory requirements with something other than

what the statute actually demands. PURA’s text requires consumer-cost evidence. Applicants

provided none.

      VI. PURA Allows Reliability-Only Projects Without a Congestion-Cost Analysis,
                       But Import Path 2 Is Not One of Them

20.      PURA draws a sharp, textual line between reliability-only transmission projects and

projects justified on economic or mixed grounds. The Legislature wrote two distinct commands

into § 37.056(c), and the Commission must honor both.

21.      Under § 37.056(c)(2), the Commission must consider: “the need for additional service

capacity or for improved service reliability.” Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(2).

22.      This subsection governs pure reliability projects—projects whose justification rests solely

on maintaining system stability, addressing N-1/N-2 contingencies, resolving thermal overloads,

or preventing voltage collapse. For such projects, the Commission has long held that quantified

congestion-cost savings are not required, because reliability benefits are not measured in dollars

but in operational necessity. When a project is justified exclusively as a reliability upgrade, the

Commission may approve it without an economic study.

23.      But PURA also contains § 37.056(c)(1), which requires the Commission to consider: “the

effect of the granting of the certificate on the cost to consumers.” This subsection governs




9 In re Gee, 941 F.3d 153, 170 (5th Cir. 2019) (Willett, J., concurring)
 economic or mixed-justification projects, and it demands quantified evidence of consumer

benefit—specifically, congestion-cost savings, rate impacts, and economic modeling. When a

utility invokes economic benefits, it must supply economic proof. The Legislature wrote a

consumer-cost requirement into the statute, and parties must satisfy it.

24.    Applicants cannot escape § 37.056(c)(1) by pointing to § 37.056(c)(2). The two

subsections are not interchangeable. A project cannot be justified economically without economic

evidence. And a project cannot be justified as reliability-only when the applicant repeatedly claims

economic benefits.

25.    Here, Applicants did not classify Import Path 2 as a pure reliability project. To the contrary,

they repeatedly asserted that Import Path 2 would:

                   a) reduce congestion,10
                   b) improve transfer capability,11
                   c) support economic development,12 and
                   d) provide consumer benefits.13

26.    Once Applicants invoked economic benefits, they triggered § 37.056(c)(1) and were

required to provide quantified congestion-cost savings. They provided none. As the ALJs found,

Applicants “did not present any quantified congestion-cost savings” for Import Path 2.

27.    Applicants’ reliance on ERCOT’s Permian Basin Reliability Plan cannot cure this defect.

The PBRP is a reliability study, not an economic one. ERCOT testified that it did not evaluate

congestion-cost savings, did not model rate impacts, and did not verify the load forecast it relied

upon. A reliability study cannot be repurposed into an economic justification simply because




               10 CNN Application, pp. 19,21,22,23, 25 and 26
               11 CNN Application, pp. 19,21,22,23, 25 and 26
               12 CNN Application, pp. 19,21,22,23, 25 and 26
               13 CNN Application, pp. 19,21,22,23, 25 and 26
 Applicants wish it so. As Justice Willett cautions, “Courts should not exalt form over substance.”

Zaatari v. City of Austin, 2019 WL 6336187, at 15 (Tex. 2019) (Willett, J., concurring).

28.     In short: PURA allows reliability-only projects without a congestion-cost analysis. Import

Path 2 is not one of them. Applicants invoked economic benefits but supplied no economic

evidence. The statutory text requires quantified consumer-cost analysis; Applicants provided none.

Under PURA’s plain terms, the Commission cannot lawfully find “need” without Issue 13

evidence. Justly so, the PUC is now requiring an answer to Issue 13. 14

                                             VI. Conclusion

29.     The original PFD has already found that Applicants did not supply a quantified estimate of

congestion cost savings to consumers.15

30.     Intervenors Allred and Pressley request the ALJ’s supplemental PFD preserve the factual

and evidentiary deficiency and answer the question related to Issue 13 directly and consistently as

the original PFD that “the record contains no evidence quantifying either [economic tests and

congestion cost savings].”16 As follows, Allred and Pressley request an amended proposal for

decision finding that Applicants have failed to establish estimated consumer congestion cost

savings attributable to the proposed transmission line facilities Import Path 2 and subsequently

issue a denial of the project on those grounds.

31.     Issue 13 is not a box to check; it is a statutory safeguard. Applicants’ failure to provide any

congestion-cost savings or rate-impact analysis leaves the Commission with no lawful basis to




14 PUC Remand Order at 2–3 (PUC 9/18/26 Document 6578).
15 PFD at 149-150 and Footnote 580; proposed Findings of Fact 226–227.
16 PFD at 150 paragraph 1.
 conclude that Import Path 2 is necessary or beneficial to Texans. Because of all the reasons

presented supra, the CCN Application must be denied.

                                            PRAYER

       Intervenors, Leif Allred and Laura Pressley respectfully request that the ALJs issue a an

amended PFD expressly answering Preliminary Order Issue13; find that estimated consumer

congestion savings attributable to these facilities have not been established; preserve the adverse

findings on need supported by the record; and recommend denial of the applications comprising

Import Path 2. Leif Allred and Laura Pressley request all further relief within the scope of remand

to which they are entitled.
